Q: How to make GitHub actions/checkout always merge into main/master tip instead of main/master past? A:

This is simply not possible. There is nothing in the documentation of actions/checkout to update the /pull/NUMBER/merge reference, or to make actions/checkout do the merge using the actual heads of pull request and default branches.

There are two alternatives, though. If you do need the SSH stuff that actions/checkout creates (which enables your scripts to run authenticated git commands), then it is possible to to "remerge" the shallow clone of actions/checkout, ignoring the outdated reference. And if you do not need the authentication stuff, it is possible to "recreate" a version of actions/checkout that does the merge in plain git commands.

  1. Re-merge the clone

    The result of a actions/checkout is a shallow clone with no history, so most commands will simply not work. We first start by fetching the commit history, without any trees or files for now (as to minimize download traffic), and then proceed to set up the bare minimum necessary to fetch and checkout the two branch tips, and finally redo the merge ourselves.

          - name: Re-merge the pull request checkout
        run: |
          # Script
          # Bases on https://stackoverflow.com/questions/79997327/

          set -x
          cd [PATH]

          git fetch -q --filter=tree:0 origin $GITHUB_BASE_REF
          git fetch -q --filter=tree:0 origin ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
          git checkout -q $GITHUB_BASE_REF

          git config user.name  "$GITHUB_ACTOR"
          git config user.email "$GITHUB_ACTOR@users.noreply.github.com"
          mainsha=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
          message="Merge ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} into ${mainsha}"

          git merge -q -m "$message" ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}

  2. Check out the merged pull request, in plain git

    Below is a recreation of most of what actions/checkout@v7 do, up to the auth stuff.

          - name: Shallow clone and merge the pull request, in plain git
        run: |
          # Script
          # Bases on https://stackoverflow.com/questions/79997327/

          repo=https://github.com/[ORG]/[REPO].git
          path=[PATH]

          set -x
          mkdir "$path"
          cd    "$path"

          git init -q .
          git config gc.auto 0
          git remote add origin "$repo"

          git fetch -q --filter=tree:0 origin $GITHUB_BASE_REF
          git fetch -q --filter=tree:0 origin ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
          git checkout -q $GITHUB_BASE_REF

          git config user.name  "$GITHUB_ACTOR"
          git config user.email "$GITHUB_ACTOR@users.noreply.github.com"
          mainsha=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
          message="Merge ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} into ${mainsha}"

          git merge -q -m "$message" ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}```

Q: How Should a Table Reference Two Columns That Have a Many-to-Many Relationship? A:

Presuming your Brands and Suppliers tables are defined as such:

CREATE TABLE Brands (
    ID   INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name CHAR(80) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE Suppliers (
    ID   INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name CHAR(80) NOT NULL
);

Your bridge table BrandsSuppliers should be constructed this way:

CREATE TABLE BrandsSuppliers (
    BrandID    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER NOT NULL,

    PRIMARY KEY (BrandID, SupplierID),

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID)
);

We use composite primary key (BrandID, SupplierID) with each component referencing to 2 other table's PKs, that is the simplest way to ensure itself's uniqueness, and it also ensure as long as a row (or pair) in this table exists, the relative brand and supplier must exist. We can of course create its own primary key ID but since this table totally depends on the other two, there's no point to add another new column for such purpose. Also, using a separate stand-alone PK would requires us to add another constraint to ensure the row's uniqueness. (explained below)

And this is how your Products table can directly reference the bridge table (AKA junction table):

CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID         INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name       CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandID    INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    CONSTRAINT FK_Product_BrandSupplier
        FOREIGN KEY (BrandID, SupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(BrandID, SupplierID)
);

It's quite straightforward. However, there are times when we need to write queries which need to JOIN between Products and Brands tables, or bwteen Products and Suppliers table. Without direct FK/PK relationship between the two tables, it's still valid to use JOIN clause but it would not leverage the relationship directly. So it would be a better idea to add the FK/PK relationship between Products and Brands, as well as between Products and Suppliers, like so:

CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID         INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name       CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandID    INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_Product_BrandSupplier
        FOREIGN KEY (BrandID, SupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(BrandID, SupplierID)
);

Adding the 2 FK references also makes relationship clearer for those who read the schema.

What if BrandsSuppliers has its own PK column

It can have its own primary key, maybe like this way:

CREATE TABLE BrandsSuppliers (
    ID         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    BrandID    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID),

    CONSTRAINT UQ_BrandSupplier UNIQUE (BrandID, SupplierID)  -- needed by many-to-many relationship
);

We need to add that UNIQUE constraint to ensure the row (relationship) is unqiue because many-to-many relationship demands that.

And now we might be tempted to change the design of Products table like so:

-- NOTE: this is a bad idea
CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID              INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name            CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandID         INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    SupplierID      INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    BrandSupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)         REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID)      REFERENCES Suppliers(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (BrandSupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(ID)
);

However, this would bring a new problem. It is highly possible that the certain product could reference to a book not in the brand-supplier relationship, or the supplier is missing in the relationship. This is problematic. We are thus forced to remove those 2 FK/PK relationship and consequently the 2 columns as well, like so:

-- Better, but not good enough.
CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID              INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name            CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandSupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandSupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(ID)
);

That means if we need to look up a product's brand info or the supplier info, we must route through the BrandsSuppliers table first. It would be 2 JOIN clauses instead of just 1. So, using composite primary key in BrandsSuppliers table is a better solution.

Q: git push fails using maven release plugin A:

See the Github documentation: Dealing with non-fast-forward errors
https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-git/dealing-with-non-fast-forward-errors

"You can fix this by fetching and merging the changes made on the remote branch with the changes that you have made locally:"

$ git fetch origin
# Fetches updates made to an online repository
$ git merge origin YOUR_BRANCH_NAME
# Merges updates made online with your local work

Q: Stepping through a TCP/IP stack A:

Mongoose https://github.com/cesanta/mongoose/ is an embedded TCP/IP stack that ships in just 2 files, mongoose.c and mongoose.h. Works under RTOS or bare metal. It has a 2-hour long video that talks through the driver and stack internals, explaining every layer:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x5Uy-CIz33k

A simple HTTP server is created on a Nucleo-F756ZG dev board using Cube IDE and Mongoose Library. Then, an HTTP request is wiretapped, and every frame gets explained - how it is handled by the embedded stack, from a driver layer, up to the application.

Q: VSCode Spring Initializr Error: Can running but package and import still red A:

If the Spring Boot app runs successfully but package and import lines are still red, I’d first suspect the VS Code Java language server rather than Spring itself.

Try these in order:

  • Make sure you opened the project folder containing pom.xml, not just the src folder.

  • Run mvn clean and then refresh/reimport the Maven project in VS Code.

  • Check that VS Code is using the same JDK version configured for the project.

  • If the errors remain, use Java: Clean Java Language Server Workspace from the Command Palette and restart VS Code.

If Maven can resolve the dependencies and the application starts normally, that’s a strong indication the project itself is fine and VS Code’s dependency/index state is stale.

If it still happens after a clean workspace, the pom.xml and the exact red error shown by VS Code would be useful to identify the specific issue.

Q: How to use js modules from non-module files A:

I spent several hours trying to find a way to call the JavaScript "module" code from the "non-module" part, which in my case was the "<script></script>" in the existing HTML page with the existing functionality. And because of the original design constraints, there was no way I was able to change the original HMTL "<script>" part to the module nature. Interestingly enough the solution provided in this post was the only one that worked for me. In other words, citing the original post "Just import all the modules, which you want to access, and attach them to the window object. Since the window object is available globally, you can access your module from anywhere ...".

I do hope it will be helpful to others who faced the same problem.
